title: Ames places faith essentially in will alone (five concurrents)
source_text: X. Sed hoc misso, quod spectat facultatem cui fides inhaeret, reperiuntur inter Theologos Reformatos nonnulli qui putant illam non esse mentem, sive intellectum, sed voluntatem solam. Omnes enim illos actus quibus proprie constat fides nolunt esse actus mentis, sed voluntatis. Haec est sententia Guil. Amesii in Medulla Theologiae, lib. 2. cap. 5. num. 12. & seqq. Postquam enim dixit quinque ad fidem concurrere, quorum primum est, Notitia rei testatae: 2. Affectio pia erga Deum, quae facit ut maxime valeat apud nos ipsius testimonium: 3. Assensus qui praebetur veritati testatae: 4. Acquiescentia in Deo ad illud quod proponitur consequendum: & 5. Electio vel apprehensio rei ipsius quae in testimonio nobis exhibetur: subjungit, Primum horum est in intellectu, sed non constituit fidem. Secundum, quartum, & quintum sunt in voluntate, & constituunt fidem. Tertium est in intellectu, sed prout movetur a voluntate, neque est proprie fidei virtus, sed effectum. Unde patet illum ita fidem in voluntate collocare secundum propriam formam & essentiam, ut tamen aliquos actus in intellectu praerequirat, & quidam etiam illius effectus ad intellectum pertineant; ut quasi e diametro sententia ejus primae supra relatae opponatur.
pass_a_gloss: But setting that aside: as to the faculty in which faith inheres, some Reformed theologians think it is not the mind or intellect but the will alone. For they refuse to count as mind-acts those acts of which faith properly consists; they want them to be will-acts. This is William Ames's opinion in Medulla Theologiae 2.5 nn.12ff. After saying five things concur to faith — (1) knowledge of the attested thing; (2) pious affection toward God making His testimony weigh most; (3) assent given to attested truth; (4) resting in God for what is proposed to be obtained; (5) election or apprehension of the thing itself exhibited in the testimony — he adds: The first is in intellect but does not constitute faith. The second, fourth, and fifth are in the will and constitute faith. The third is in intellect as moved by the will, and is not properly faith's virtue but an effect. Whence it is clear he seats faith in the will as to its proper form and essence, though he presupposes some intellect-acts and allows some effects to touch intellect — almost diametrically opposite the first opinion related above.
pass_b_english: Ames (Medulla 2.5): faith's constituting acts are will-acts; knowledge does not constitute; assent is effect.
Essentially in will alone — nearly the reverse of the intellect-only party.

choices.why: Make up faith's essence for Ames.
